video_title: Why Crypto’s Options Market Might Finally Take Off
gist: Nick Forester, co-founder and CEO of the onchain options exchange Derive, argues crypto options are at an inflection point: they sit at only 3-4% of crypto perp volume versus rough parity in TradFi, implying 30-40x of headroom, and the October 10 ("1010") crash was the catalyst by destroying the basis trade and pre-TGE token-yield games while exposing perps' path dependency. He lays out the economics of options exchanges (roughly 3bps taker fees, stronger liquidity network effects than perps, Deribit at 70-75% share), Derive's wedge of listing new assets first (Hyperliquid options in November at $20 HYPE), and second-order effects: dampened volatility, options becoming a mandatory exchange offering, and "DeFi mullet" structured products embedded in neobanks and overcollateralized stablecoins.

insights.claim: Options are structurally the last vertical to mature in any new asset class because they require slow-moving anchor participants — institutions selling options for yield, or structural hedgers like airlines hedging jet fuel and farmers hedging crops — to create a competitive two-way market, not just speculators.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Use the presence of repeat institutional yield-sellers and hedgers, not retail speculative volume, as the leading indicator for when a crypto options venue is about to inflect.
insights.quote: Options are always the last vertical to mature.

insights.claim: Crypto options could not develop because the tradeable asset set was too narrow and too ephemeral — meme coins that dominated perp trading last two or three weeks, which is not long enough for a double coincidence of wants to form around dated strikes.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Options liquidity should follow assets with long-lived, sophisticated holder bases and large market caps — screen new listings on that profile rather than on raw perp volume.

insights.claim: The incumbent liquidity leader in crypto options built a strong business but never modernized its user interface or expanded beyond big institutional OTC desks, leaving the broader retail and builder audience structurally unserved until now.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: The addressable opening in crypto options is distribution and UX, not raw liquidity — watch for challengers that win the retail/builder layer rather than the OTC desk layer.

themes.theme: October 10 crash as the options catalyst

insights.claim: The October 10 ("1010") crash of last year was a step change for crypto options demand, which was near zero across the board beforehand, because it demonstrated that perp traders can be fully delta neutral and correctly risk-managed and still be liquidated by a downside wick.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Post-1010 options demand is a behavioral regime change, not a fad — expect options share of crypto derivatives volume to ratchet rather than mean-revert.
insights.quote: you can do everything right and be delta neutral and manage your risk and yet still get blown out on on like a scam wick to the downside

insights.claim: The 1010 crash killed the crypto basis trade as a yield source by wiping out industry leverage and resetting funding rates, destroying the track records of hedge funds, family offices and liquid funds that had built four-year trajectories on 10-15% delta-neutral returns.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Allocators who previously underwrote 10-15% delta-neutral basis yield now need a replacement sleeve, and options premium selling is the stated substitute — a demand tailwind for options venues.
insights.quote: there were a lot of like hedge funds, family offices, liquid funds that had built their entire like four-year trajectory and like track record on earning, you know, 10 to 15% delta neutral and that went up in in flames on 1010

insights.claim: The second yield source 1010 destroyed was the pre-TGE game in which teams sold tokens before launch to inflate TVL and promised investors a native-token yield hedged out through OTC markets or premarket points venues — token valuations were crushed and the trade stopped working.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Protocols whose TVL was manufactured by pre-TGE point-farming yield are structurally impaired post-1010; treat their historical TVL growth as non-recurring.

insights.claim: For roughly the last year, selling options has been essentially the only place to earn yield in crypto at institutional scale, and that has been sustainable rather than a transient dislocation.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Volatility selling is the current marginal source of institutional crypto yield — crowding here is the risk factor to monitor, and it is what will compress implied vol over time.

insights.claim: A live trade on Derive shows the convexity case: a buyer of the ETH March 2027 5,000/7,000 call spread paid about $300,000 in premium for a payoff of roughly $20 million if ETH reaches $7K by March — about a 66x payout with ETH near $2,500 at the time of recording.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Long-dated call spreads let a fund express a high-conviction multi-month upside view with defined, pre-paid risk and no liquidation path — a capital-efficient substitute for leveraged spot or perps.
insights.quote: he has put down $300,000 worth of premiums. If ETH goes to 7K by March, that call spread will pay out about $20 million.

insights.claim: Replicating that 66x payoff with a perp is impossible: $1,000 at 66x leverage creates a $66,000 ETH position that is instantly liquidated on a 1.5% drawdown from spot, and at roughly 10% funding costs about $6,600 a year — six times the margin posted.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the carry-plus-path-dependency tax on high-leverage perps and gives a concrete threshold above which options strictly dominate for directional expression.
insights.quote: You just can't express that view in any way, shape, or form using the perbs.

insights.claim: On 1010 the traders who were wiped out were not running reckless leverage but 1.25x to 1.5x, and even correlation-hedged books — long one alt, short another, or long Bitcoin short ETH — were auto-deleveraged when exchange infrastructure and liquidity became shaky.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Perp exposure carries venue and ADL risk that low leverage does not neutralize — a reason to price exchange infrastructure risk separately from market risk.

insights.claim: Options and perps are complementary rather than competing instruments: perps are a blunt instrument good for price discovery, pre-market listings and short-dated speculation, while options function as a Swiss Army knife for structured products, yield generation and fine-tuned hedging, and Derive cross-margins both.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: The 'perps killed options' narrative is wrong on the venue level — the durable winner is the exchange that cross-margins both, which is also the hardest architecture to retrofit.
insights.quote: Options are much more like a Swiss Army knife.

insights.claim: Crypto options are only about 3-4% of the size of the crypto perp market while in traditional finance options are roughly the same size as or slightly larger than futures, implying roughly 30-40x of growth for crypto options just to reach TradFi parity.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: This is the headline TAM ratio for sizing crypto options venues and their tokens — a 30-40x structural gap versus an already-mature perp market.
insights.quote: We're like 3% or 4% of the per market and in Tradfi they're about the same if not options being slightly bigger.

insights.claim: Roughly half of traditional options activity never prints on an exchange because it clears as OTC bilateral deals, meaning reported exchange volume understates the real market by about 2x, with total notional in the quadrillions and single market makers earning three to four billion dollars of profit in a quarter.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Exchange-reported volume is the wrong denominator for sizing the options opportunity — onchain venues that convert OTC flow via RFQ capture the hidden half.
insights.quote: It's in the quadrillions of notional volume.

insights.claim: Options exchanges have stronger liquidity network effects than perp exchanges because the anchor institutional participants who build the market are slow-moving, which is why the incumbent kept its stranglehold even when Binance attacked in 2020 with more liquid perps.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Options market share, once won on a given asset, is far stickier than perp share — first-to-list on a new asset is the durable moat, and cheap capital alone cannot buy it.
insights.quote: There are stronger network effects around options exchanges um even more so than per

themes.theme: Deribit's moat and Derive's listing wedge

insights.claim: Deribit still holds roughly 70-75% of crypto options volume, with Bullish, Bybit and OKX making funded but limited inroads, so the sector remains close to a single-venue monopoly.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Concentration this extreme means share shifts are the key observable — track new-asset listing races rather than headline volume for early signal.
insights.quote: So Darabit I think are still like 70 75% of the market.

insights.claim: Derive went from about 0.15% market share a year to eighteen months ago to a meaningful position by listing Hyperliquid options in November of last year when HYPE traded around $20, becoming the only and then the most liquid global venue for HYPE options and pulling flow away from OTC desks.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Demonstrates the first-mover listing playbook working in practice — Deribit launched HYPE options only about two months ago and Derive still holds the majority of that volume.
insights.quote: we listed Hyperlquid options um in November last year when Hype was at $20

insights.claim: Derive intends to run the same first-to-list playbook across every new asset with a sophisticated long-term holder base and a large market cap, including tokenized RWAs, equities and commodities, and claims it already has the most alt markets and the biggest Solana options market while being competitive in Bitcoin and ETH.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: The tokenized-RWA wave is the next options listing frontier; the venue that lists these first inherits the sticky options network effect for that asset.

insights.claim: Derive runs a hybrid architecture — an off-chain order book and integrated RFQ written in Rust for low-latency matching and price discovery, with self-custodial portfolio margin, clearing and settlement executed in smart contracts — and claims this is now competitive with centralized exchanges on merit alone.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: The winning onchain derivatives design keeps matching off-chain and risk/settlement on-chain — a template for judging competing DEX architectures.

insights.claim: Derive's onchain portfolio margin runs a user's full account through 27 risk scenarios — for example spot up 20% with volatility to 100% — and charges the worst-case loss as margin, with liquidations handled by a permissionless onchain Dutch auction that decays from a small discount toward 100%, then a fee-funded onchain insurance fund, then transparent ADL rules.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: A fully verifiable risk waterfall is the concrete differentiator onchain venues can market to institutions burned by opaque CEX liquidation and ADL behavior.
insights.quote: it runs it through 27 different risk scenarios

insights.claim: Derive's V3, due in about a month, is positioned to make the protocol integrable in an hour of work, with a major margin-system upgrade, multi-asset borrow-lend, and the ability to deploy structured products, quantitative strategy vaults and copy-trading vaults in three clicks.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: A near-dated catalyst — if integration friction really drops to an hour, third-party builder volume becomes the measurable proof point to watch after launch.

themes.theme: Second-order effects of liquid crypto options

insights.claim: As crypto options markets become liquid, realized and implied volatility should generally fall, because option sellers stuff dealers with vol and gamma that dealers must then hedge, producing a market-wide dampening effect.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Structurally lower crypto vol compresses returns for vol-selling and basis strategies but makes the asset class more investable for size-constrained institutions.
insights.quote: when our options markets become liquid, volatility actually generally comes down

insights.claim: Options will become a mandatory offering for crypto exchanges, but retrofitting a perp risk engine to support options is very hard — cross-margined options must be designed in from day one — so the likely outcome is a wave of white-labeling and integrations rather than in-house builds.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Creates a B2B infrastructure market: venues that already cross-margin options and perps can rent their risk engine to every perp exchange that cannot rebuild one.
insights.quote: It's really hard to retrofit a per risk engine to add options.

insights.claim: The 'DeFi mullet' end state for options is packaged payoffs sold through consumer front ends — a neobank offering roughly 8% annually from a backtested covered-call-spread selling strategy with a defined maximum drawdown of about 1% in a given week or month — democratizing products currently reserved for high-net-worth private wealth.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: The monetization layer sits with integrators who mark up the payoff, not the exchange charging 3bps — the value accrual question for options infrastructure tokens.
insights.quote: you can earn 8% annually back tested uh with this options covered call spread selling strategy with a maximum defined draw down of like 1% in a given week or a given month

insights.claim: Tokenized stocks currently have almost no onchain utility beyond lending and borrowing against them, which makes them a natural first market for options-based yield generation once options infrastructure supports them as collateral.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Options are the missing yield primitive for tokenized equities — watch whether RWA adoption accelerates once covered-call style products exist on them.

insights.claim: Large options flow can mechanically move underlying prices via dealer hedging — the Archegos episode saw one participant single-handedly push the NASDAQ higher through calls and call spreads on names like Microsoft, Google and CRM — but markets are weighing machines, so gains unsupported by fundamentals reverse, making the durable effect on crypto prices more muted than tighter spreads and lower volatility.
insights.speaker: Nick Forester (co-founder and CEO, Derive)
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the assumption that an options volume boom is directly bullish for spot — the real benefit is execution quality and investability, not a sustained price bid.
insights.quote: He was single-handedly moving the NASDAQ with his options trades
